evidence_in_original: PDF trang 41 (in 21): đoạn văn: "The Human Capital Index is 0.85 for children in the richest 20 percent of households, compared to 0.58 for children in the poorest 20 percent" || PDF trang 41 (in 21): đoạn văn: "the gap in the Human Capital Index between the top 20 and bottom 20 in Vietnam is 0.27 points, higher than the average gap among 50 countries (0.15 points)"
agent_answer:
Children in the richest 20 percent of households have a Human Capital Index (HCI) of 0.85, compared with 0.58 for children in the poorest 20 percent. The gap is 0.27 points [pea-p041-t01]. Vietnam's gap is larger than the average gap of 0.15 points across 50 countries in the D'Souza, Gatti, and Kraay (2019) comparison [pea-p041-t01]. The report also says gaps in Vietnam between the bottom and top 20 percent are larger than average for several outcomes, including the SES-disaggregated HCI, test scores and stunting [pea-p031-t01].

The report also expresses the same SES-HCI gap relative to the average: children in the poorest 20 percent score 17 points below the average, and children in the richest 20 percent score 16 percent above it [pea-p134-t03]. This is a different normalization from the 0.85 and 0.58 figures, so I have not combined them.

question: In which SEDP phases were the poor and near-poor determined by household income only?
expected_answer: In the 2006–2010 and 2011–2015 phases.
evidence_in_original: PDF trang 70 (in 50): đoạn văn: "For the 2006–2010 and 2011–2015 phases, the poor and near-poor were determined by only household income"
agent_answer: The poor and near-poor were determined by household income only in the 2006–2010 and 2011–2015 SEDP phases [pea-p070-t03] (PDF page 70). From 2016 to 2020, the poor were still identified by a low monetary threshold based on household income, but the near-poor also had to be deprived in 3 of 10 non-monetary indicators, so that phase used a combination of monetary and non-monetary criteria [pea-p070-t04] (PDF page 70).
